extraction.name: CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100
extraction.description: Two manually labeled subsets of the 80 million tiny images dataset, containing 32×32 colour images. CIFAR-10 contains 60,000 images in 10 classes, with 6,000 images per class. CIFAR-100 contains 60,000 images in 100 classes, with 600 images per class, organized into 20 superclasses of five classes each. The CIFAR-100 classes are mutually exclusive with the CIFAR-10 classes.
extraction.creator: Alex Krizhevsky; Vinod Nair is acknowledged for a substantial contribution to the labeling project.
extraction.inLanguage: English class names and source search terms.
extraction.citeAs: Alex Krizhevsky. Learning Multiple Layers of Features from Tiny Images. April 8, 2009.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The source tiny images dataset was collected by colleagues at MIT and NYU over six months. They searched the web for every non-abstract English noun in WordNet using several search engines, including Google, Flickr, and Altavista, retaining roughly the first 3,000 results per search term. Perfect duplicates and images with an excessively large proportion of white pixels were removed. To construct CIFAR-10, paid students examined images retrieved using each assigned class name and its WordNet hyponyms, rejecting images that did not meet the class inclusion criteria. Every submitted label was personally verified by the researchers, and duplicates and near duplicates were removed. CIFAR-100 was collected using the same methodology.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Secondary Data analysis, Manual Human Curator
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The 80 million tiny images dataset: web images retrieved through Google, Flickr, Altavista, and other search engines using approximately 79,000 non-abstract English nouns from WordNet. Images were downscaled to 32×32 colour images. Each source image had a rough label corresponding to its retrieval search term.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Source images were downscaled to 32×32. CIFAR duplicates and near duplicates were removed by comparing images using the L2 norm with a rejection threshold sufficiently liberal to detect re-saved JPEGs as well as perfect duplicates. CIFAR-10 was divided into training and test sets, with 5,000 randomly selected images per class assigned to training and the remaining 1,000 per class assigned to testing.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Source collection filtering removed perfect duplicates and images with an excessively large proportion of white pixels, which tended to be synthetic figures. Human filtering removed mislabeled or otherwise unsuitable images from the labeled subsets. For model experiments, the paper describes ZCA whitening to remove second-order pixel correlations and deletion of the 1,000 least-significant principal components to reduce high-frequency noise. The principal-component deletion was retained for subsequent experiments, including experiments on unwhitened data. Patch-based experiments divided each 32×32 image into 25 overlapping 8×8 patches and created an additional 8×8 subsampled version of the whole image.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Paid student labelers were assigned a class and examined source images retrieved with that class name and its WordNet hyponyms, rejecting images outside the class. The class name should be a likely basic-category answer to what the main object is. Images generally needed one prominent object and a photorealistic appearance; line drawings and cartoons were rejected, while sufficiently photorealistic drawings with internal texture could be accepted. Unusual viewpoints, partial occlusion, and cluttered or uniform backgrounds were acceptable when object identity remained clear. False positives were considered worse than false negatives. Ambiguous category names were restricted to their main meaning, with labelers instructed to ask when uncertain. For plural CIFAR-100 class names, labelers were instructed not to reject images containing multiple instances. Labelers received a fixed hourly payment, and researchers personally verified every submitted label.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The source search-term labels were described as extremely unreliable. Human labelers filtered out mislabeled images, and the researchers personally verified every submitted label. Instructions prioritized avoiding false positives over avoiding false negatives and advised labelers to assess whether they could identify the object without priming. Duplicate and near-duplicate removal followed labeling.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: CIFAR-100 includes a people superclass with the class labels baby, boy, girl, man, and woman.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The source images exhibit vertical and horizontal symmetry and stronger correlations between distant pixels in the same row or column. The paper suggests this is probably caused by photographic practices such as keeping the ground plane horizontal and centering the main object. Labeling instructions explicitly favor excluding uncertain images rather than including false positives, and generally exclude images with multiple equally prominent objects and non-photorealistic depictions.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The source tiny images dataset has extremely unreliable search-term labels, making it difficult to use directly for object-recognition experiments. CIFAR inclusion criteria generally restrict images to clearly identifiable, photorealistic objects with one prominent instance, with an exception for plural CIFAR-100 classes. CIFAR-10 automobile and truck classes exclude pickup trucks; pickup truck is a separate CIFAR-100 class. All reported object-classification experiments used CIFAR-10 because CIFAR-100 had only recently been completed.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Supervised object-recognition training and testing using the reliable CIFAR labels. CIFAR-10 provides a randomly selected training split of 5,000 images per class and a test split of 1,000 images per class. The source tiny images dataset was used for unsupervised training of RBMs and deep generative models, typically using about two million images, followed by supervised classifier training and fine-tuning on CIFAR-10. CIFAR-100 classes can be used as negative examples for CIFAR-10 because the class sets are mutually exclusive. CIFAR-100 superclass groupings organize similar classes that are intended to be harder to distinguish than classes from different superclasses.
